title: Only 600 mL out
note: Fictional patient. Troubleshooting follows the unit protocol; laxatives, solution changes and imaging are prescriber decisions.
intro: You are the PD nurse on the evening hotline. At 19:00, Mrs. Corazon Dela Cruz, 52, on CAPD (continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis) for four months, calls. Her drain has been running for 30 minutes and only 600 mL has come out of a 2,000 mL fill. “What should I do?”

choices.text: Screen first: breathing, pain, effluent, bowels, and when it started.
choices.feedback: The breathing question comes before the position question. A slow drain in a comfortable patient can be troubleshot; a slow drain in a breathless patient is an emergency.
choices.then: She is comfortable, breathing normally, the effluent is clear, and she has not moved her bowels in four days. The problem started with this drain.

choices.text: Ask her to stand, walk around and lean to each side, since a displaced catheter is the most common cause of a slow drain.
choices.feedback: Position changes are often the answer, but only after you know she is stable. Ask about breathing, pain and effluent first.
choices.then: You go back and ask: she is comfortable, breathing normally, the effluent is clear, and she has not moved her bowels in four days.

choices.text: Tell her to come to the unit.
choices.feedback: She may need to come in, but you cannot know yet. A few questions tell you whether this is an emergency or something she can fix at home.
choices.then: You ask first: she is comfortable, breathing normally, the effluent is clear, and she has not moved her bowels in four days.

n2.scene: Her daughter, a nursing student, is with her and offers to flush the catheter with a syringe of saline.
n2.prompt: What do you ask them to do?

choices.text: Check the clamps and line for kinks, check bag height, then walk and change position. No syringe.
choices.feedback: These are the permitted steps when the patient is stable. Forceful flushing can push a fibrin plug deeper, tear tissue or bring in bacteria; it is done only when ordered, by someone trained.
choices.then: The clamps are open and the line is straight. After ten minutes of walking and leaning, the drain picks up.

choices.text: Let her daughter flush gently with 20 mL of sterile saline.
choices.feedback: Flushing is not permitted at home unless ordered and trained for this catheter. Force can make a fixable problem permanent.
choices.then: The flush meets resistance and Mrs. Dela Cruz feels a pull. You stop them and ask for clamps, kinks and position changes instead; the drain slowly picks up.

choices.text: Do the next fill now and drain later.
choices.feedback: Filling on top of retained fluid raises pressure in the abdomen and risks overload or leaks. Work out why it is not draining first.
choices.then: You stop her before she connects the new bag, and walk her through clamps, kinks and position changes. The drain picks up.

n3.scene: “My neighbor says to take two sachets of a strong laxative from the drugstore tonight. Should I?”

choices.text: Not on her own: you will report the constipation to the team for a bowel plan.
choices.feedback: Constipation is a common cause of outflow failure, because a full bowel pushes the catheter tip out of place. The bowel plan is a prescriber decision; some laxatives are not safe in kidney failure. Report it the same day and teach her to log her drain volumes.
choices.then: The team orders a bowel plan that evening; you call her back with it.

choices.text: Yes, take them tonight, since clearing the bowel is the fastest way to get the catheter draining well again.
choices.feedback: The reasoning is right, but the choice of laxative is the prescriber’s. Some over-the-counter products contain phosphate or magnesium, which are risky in kidney failure.
choices.then: You call back before she takes them, with the bowel plan the team ordered.

choices.text: Eat more fiber, vegetables and fruit, and drink more water, which usually gets the bowels moving within a day or two.
choices.feedback: Fiber helps, but more water may not suit her fluid allowance, and four days without a movement needs a bowel plan from the team.
choices.then: You report it, and the team orders a bowel plan.

n4.scene: Mrs. Dela Cruz calls again. Her bowels are moving and the drains are fine, but her right side feels heavy and she gets short of breath after every fill. After draining she feels better. Her drain volumes have fallen since yesterday.

choices.text: No more fills tonight. You are calling the team urgently.
choices.feedback: Breathlessness after fills that eases after draining, with a heavy right side and falling drains, suggests dialysate leaking into the chest (a pleural leak). That is urgent: stop fills and call. If she is breathless at rest, she goes through the emergency pathway.
choices.then: The nephrologist on duty asks for her to be seen tonight.

choices.text: Try a stronger bag tonight to pull more fluid off, since falling drains and breathlessness can mean fluid overload.
choices.feedback: Changing the solution is a prescription decision. And if fluid is leaking into the chest, more fills make it worse whatever the strength.
choices.then: You think again, tell her not to fill, and call the team urgently.

choices.text: Come in at the next clinic day.
choices.feedback: A possible pleural leak cannot wait for clinic. Stop fills and call the team now.
choices.then: You think again, tell her not to fill, and call the team urgently.

n5.prompt: What do you tell the nephrologist?

choices.text: SBAR: breathless after fills, easing after drains, heavy right side, falling drains, breathing now.
choices.feedback: The pattern (which phase, where the fluid seems to go) names the likely mechanism. Add how she is breathing right now, her last completed exchange, Tuesday’s slow drain, the bowel plan, and what you told her.
The nephrologist needs the facts that led you there, and how she is breathing right now, to decide how fast to act.

choices.text: Her full story since she started PD four months ago, every call to the hotline, and the details of her training.
choices.feedback: Complete but slow. Lead with the current problem and her state now; the background can follow.

end.title: The next morning
end.text: A chest X-ray shows fluid on the right side. The team pauses PD and arranges temporary hemodialysis while they decide what comes next. You document both calls, and at her next visit you review her go-bag and her plan for missed therapy.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Screen before you troubleshoot: breathing, pain, effluent, bowels.
  • Permitted steps only: clamps, kinks, bag height, position. No syringe at home.
  • Constipation is a common cause of a slow drain; the bowel plan comes from the prescriber.
  • Ask which phase the problem happens in. Breathless after fills suggests a pleural leak: stop fills and call.

See Mechanisms, Assess first and Safe troubleshooting.
